Everything here is invented. kind: note (their own words) | link (a saved article: collected, not their view).

notes.title: Espresso dial-in log
notes.summary: Dial-in settings for the Ethiopian beans on the home espresso machine.
notes.text:
Dialled in the Ethiopian Guji today after three sour shots.

What finally worked: grinder setting 14, 18 g in, 38 g out in 29 seconds. Water at 93 °C. Anything coarser than 15 ran fast and tasted thin.

Next bag: start at 14 again and only move one step at a time. The Colombian needed setting 11 last month, so do not assume.

notes.title: Kiln firing schedule – cone 6
notes.summary: The glaze firing schedule that stopped the pinholing.
notes.text:
Glaze firing schedule that fixed the pinholes:

- 100 °C per hour to 600 °C
- 150 °C per hour to 1100 °C
- 60 °C per hour to 1222 °C, hold 15 minutes
- Controlled cool at 80 °C per hour down to 900 °C, then off

Bisque stays at 1000 °C. The slow cool is what gave the celadon its depth. One kiln load a week is plenty.

notes.title: Sourdough starter notes
notes.summary: How I keep the starter (Clint) alive and when it peaks.
notes.text:
The starter is called Clint. Feed ratio 1:5:5 (starter, water, flour) with 20% rye in the flour. At kitchen temperature it peaks in about 9 hours; in the fridge I feed it once a week.

If it smells like nail polish it is hungry, not dead. Bake when it has doubled and a spoonful floats.

notes.title: French lesson – the subjunctive
notes.summary: My own notes on when French uses the subjunctive.
notes.text:
Camille's rule of thumb for the subjunctive: it follows doubt, desire, emotion and necessity. 'Il faut que tu viennes.' 'Je veux que tu saches.'

My mistake every week: using it after 'espérer', which takes the indicative. After 'penser que' it is indicative when affirmative and subjunctive when negative.

Homework for Thursday: ten sentences with 'bien que'.

notes.title: Meeting – Halvorsen kitchen project
notes.summary: Kick-off meeting notes for the Halvorsen kitchen: budget, deadline, supplier.
notes.text:
Kick-off with Ingrid Halvorsen.

Budget agreed at 48,500 all in. Deadline for install is March 6. Cabinets come from Brandt & Lowe, six-week lead time, so the order has to go in this week.

She wants oak fronts, no handles, and the tall unit moved to the north wall. Open question: whether the old floor stays. I estimated 4 working weeks on site; the actual figure will depend on the floor.

notes.title: Thoughts on slow work
notes.summary: Why I would rather do fewer things with more attention.
notes.text:
I keep coming back to the idea that speed is a way of not looking. When I rush a piece I stop seeing it; I only see the list.

I would rather make four things a month that I have really looked at than twenty I cannot remember. Slowness is not laziness. It is the price of attention.

The hard part is saying no early, before the calendar says it for me.

notes.title: Why I quit daily word counts
notes.summary: Counting words made me write worse; what I do instead.
notes.text:
For two years I logged a daily word count. It made me productive and it made the writing worse: I padded to hit the number.

Now I measure sessions, not words. One honest hour counts, even if it ends with fewer words than it started with. The count rewarded speed, and speed was the problem.

notes.title: Studio rules
notes.summary: The handful of rules I work by in the studio.
notes.text:
1. No phone before noon.
2. One kiln load a week.
3. Finish the piece on the bench before starting the next.
4. Friday afternoon is for cleaning, not making.
5. If I am rushing, stop and sweep the floor.

notes.title: Running log – my definitions
notes.summary: What I mean by easy, tempo and long runs.
notes.text:
My own definitions, so the log stays consistent:

- Easy run: anything I could do while talking.
- Tempo: 20 minutes at the pace I could hold for an hour.
- Long run: anything over 8 km. That is short by most people's standards, but it is my line.

This week: two easy, one long (9.5 km on Sunday).

notes.title: Sleep experiments
notes.summary: What I tried for sleep and what seemed to help.
notes.text:
Three weeks of notes.

Magnesium glycinate, 300 mg before bed: fell asleep faster on most nights, though it is only my impression. No screens after ten helped more. Coffee after 2 pm clearly hurt.

Not tried yet: cooler bedroom.

notes.title: Pour-over vs espresso – my take
notes.summary: Why I still prefer espresso at home but pour-over on weekends.
notes.text:
I like pour-over for light roasts: it shows the fruit that espresso crushes. But on a weekday I want the ritual to take two minutes, so espresso wins.

My honest view: pour-over is the better drink and espresso is the better habit.

notes.title: Pour-over coffee – brewing guide
notes.summary: A saved brewing guide for pour-over coffee.
notes.text: Pour-over coffee is brewed by pouring hot water over ground coffee in a filter. A common starting ratio is 1 gram of coffee to 16 grams of water. Water between 90 and 96 °C is typical. Bloom the grounds with twice their weight in water for 30 to 45 seconds, then pour in slow circles. Total brew time is usually between two and a half and four minutes. Many experts consider pour-over the best way to taste a single-origin coffee.

notes.title: Glaze recipe – celadon
notes.summary: The celadon glaze recipe that works at cone 6.
notes.text:
Celadon, cone 6

- Feldspar 40
- Silica 30
- Whiting 20
- Kaolin 10
- Red iron oxide 1.5

Mix ratio is 10 parts dry glaze to 9 parts water by weight. Sieve twice at 80 mesh. Apply thick on porcelain, thin on stoneware.

notes.title: Reading notes – The Overstory
notes.summary: My reactions while reading The Overstory.
notes.text:
Halfway through. The first third, the separate lives, is the best part; once the plots join it gets preachy.

What stays with me is the patience of it: trees as the slow protagonists. It made me want to do less, more carefully. Connects to what I wrote about slow work.
